section_title: What does heaven celebrate when the seventh trumpet sounds?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 15 Then the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, and loud voices called out in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever.” 16 And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, 17 saying: “We give thanks to You, O Lord God Almighty, the One who is and who was, because You have taken Your great power and have begun to reign. 18 The nations were enraged, and Your wrath has come. The time has come to judge the dead and to reward Your servants the prophets, as well as the saints and those who fear Your name, both small and great— and to destroy those who destroy the earth.”

19 Then the temple of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of His covenant appeared in His temple. And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and a great hailstorm.

context_lines: The seventh trumpet is answered by loud voices in heaven announcing that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ. The announcement brings the promise of completion in chapter 10 into focus: His reign will endure forever.

The twenty-four elders fall before God and give thanks that He has taken His great power and begun to reign. They name the conflict between the enraged nations and God’s judgment. Their praise includes the judgment of the dead, the reward of God’s servants and the destruction of those who destroy the earth.

The people named for reward include prophets, saints and all who fear God’s name, small and great. The vision does not restrict God’s recognition to people of public importance. The same scene announces accountability for those who bring destruction.

God’s heavenly temple opens, revealing the ark of His covenant. Lightning, rumblings, thunder, an earthquake and hail accompany the scene. The chapter moves from a threatened holy city and slain witnesses to heaven’s declaration of God’s enduring rule and His covenant.
common_interpretation_lines: The main readings agree that this trumpet announces God’s victory and enduring reign. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/) understands the proclamation as introducing events unfolded through the remainder of the book. [Walvoord](https://swartzentrover.com/cotor/E-Books/holiness/Walvoord/Revelation/Rev_11.htm) likewise sees an announcement of the coming kingdom before all the judgments leading to it have been narrated. Heaven celebrates the certain outcome while the vision still has more to disclose.

Teachers differ over how to arrange the later judgments and the thousand years mentioned in chapter 20. Those questions should be distinguished from the shared emphasis here: God judges evil, honors His servants and reigns through His Christ. The covenant ark is read as assurance of God’s faithfulness, rather than permission to identify a present earthly location for the lost ark.
god_plan_lines: The nations’ anger and the rule of God’s Anointed One recall [Psalm 2](https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/2.htm). There, rulers gather against the LORD and His Anointed, but their resistance cannot overturn His purpose. Revelation’s announcement carries that conflict toward its promised outcome: earthly rebellion will not determine the world’s final ruler.

The everlasting kingdom also corresponds to [Daniel 7:13–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/daniel/7.htm), where one like a son of man receives dominion over all peoples, nations and languages, and His kingdom will never be destroyed. These connections explain why the scene is a reason for worship. God’s larger purpose includes justice, the vindication of His servants and a reign that hostile powers cannot bring to an end.
